title: Protect the Punctual
author: Workshopbank
summary: Workshopbank offers facilitators a systematic approach to handling late arrivals in meetings and training sessions without penalizing the people who showed up on time. The central argument is that stopping to recap for a latecomer isn't neutral kindness, it's a signal to the entire room that punctuality carries no cost, which trains even reliable attendees to stop bothering. The piece works through eight distinct latecomer scenarios (a single person, half the group, a senior stakeholder, someone stepping out and back, a direct request to be caught up, a chronic offender, a culturally-late organization, and prevention via a pre-session message), each resolved by the same four underlying rules: never stop the group for one person, never recap in public, let materials and peers do the catching-up, and keep attention on the people who arrived on time. The piece closes by distinguishing sympathy for a latecomer's reasons from the design decision itself, arguing a facilitator can be warm to the individual while still refusing to spend the group's collective time compensating for them.
points: Argues that stopping to recap for a latecomer isn't a neutral kindness but a structural signal to the whole room that being on time carries no benefit, which erodes punctuality over repeated sessions.

Distills eight distinct latecomer scenarios (single person, half the group, a senior stakeholder, chronic offenders, and more) down to four consistent rules: never stop the group, never recap publicly, let peers and materials catch people up, and protect on-time attendees' attention.

Recommends designing the opening five minutes of a session (a written or paired activity) to be valuable for the on-time crowd but skippable without real loss for latecomers, so the schedule protects itself by design.
Distinguishes caring about a latecomer's underlying reason from the facilitation decision itself, arguing warmth toward the individual and protecting the group's collective time are not in conflict.
quotes: Watch the room while you do it. The people who were there on time just gave up three minutes so that one person could catch up. That took me too long to understand. When you stop for a latecomer you're not really helping one person. You're teaching the whole room how this session works.
The schedule belongs to the room, not to the person who's late. Everything else drops out of that. Never stop the group for one person. Never recap in public.
The second you start recapping, twelve people who heard it the first time sit through it again. You've taken their time and handed it to the person who came late, which rewards the lateness.

We start at 9:00 sharp. First activity begins immediately. Late arrivals join in where we are at. Most people run late because they assume the first ten minutes are hellos and housekeeping, the skippable part.
Protect the punctual. They're the ones deciding whether this session is worth their full effort. Give them a reason to keep showing up on time, and they will.
